title: Empty on the Road Home
sum: A famine drives Elimelech, Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem, the "house of bread," to Moab. Within ten years all three men are dead, and Naomi is left with two Moabite daughters-in-law and no grandchildren. When she hears that the LORD has given bread again, she sets out for home and tries to send the young widows back. Orpah, in tears, goes. Ruth refuses: "Where you go, I will go... your God is my God."

Back in Bethlehem the women of the town hardly know Naomi. She tells them to call her Mara, "Bitter": "Full I went out, and empty the LORD has brought me back." But it is the beginning of the barley harvest, and Ruth is standing at her side.
readings: Read as history

A real family's tragedy in the days of the judges. Famine, migration and early death were common, and a widow with no son had no secure place. Ruth's vow is a costly, legally serious decision to join a foreign people, and the chapter records how David's family line almost ended before it began.
Read as story

A carefully built short story. Its key word is shuv, "return," used twelve times. Every name means something: "My God is King" dies in a time with no king, "Pleasant" calls herself "Bitter." The chapter moves from famine to harvest and from "full" to "empty," and sets up every problem the rest of the book will solve.
Read as theology

Naomi says God has turned against her, and the narrator does not argue. Yet God "had come to help his people" (1:6), and the one person who stays with Naomi is the foreigner who has just taken Naomi's God as her own. The chapter lets lament and hidden grace sit side by side.

views.J: The rabbis taught that Elimelech was a wealthy leader who abandoned his people in the famine, and that his sons died for leaving the land and marrying Moabites (Targum; Ruth Rabbah). Ruth's vow became the model for conversion: Naomi's repeated "Go back" is read as the custom of testing a would-be convert by first turning them away (Ruth Rabbah; compare Yevamot 47b).
views.T: Ruth leaving her country for Israel's God is a picture of a Gentile coming to faith, like the nations streaming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3). Her vow is often compared to a disciple's call to follow at any cost (Luke 9:57–62), and her "return" to a land she has never seen to conversion itself.
views.R: The chapter shows how close David's family came to dying out. Conservative scholars such as Robert Hubbard and Daniel Block read it as the true background to Israel's royal house, told to show that God preserved the line through a foreign woman's loyalty.
views.E: For critical scholars who date the book after the exile (for example André LaCocque), the mixed marriages in 1:4 and Ruth's vow in 1:16 are the whole point: Ezra and Nehemiah treated Moabite wives as a threat to Israel's faith (Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:23–27); this story makes one the most faithful member of Israel.
views.W: A story of two widows with no men to protect them. Ruth chooses another woman over her own family's security, a decision Phyllis Trible argued goes beyond even Abraham's leap of faith, since Ruth had no call or promise from God. Naomi's lament gives voice to women's grief that the larger history usually leaves out.

deep.b:
The book of Judges describes a repeating cycle: Israel turns to other gods, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, God raises a judge to rescue them (Judges 2:11–19). Famine was one of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:23–24). Ruth does not say the famine was a punishment, and it never says leaving was a sin, though some Jewish tradition says both. What the narrator does say is that the famine ended when the LORD "had come to help his people" (1:6).

One of Moab's own kings, Eglon, had ruled over Israel during that era (Judges 3:12–14). So the fact that an Israelite family looked for food in Moab is itself striking.

Moab's god Chemosh is named on the Mesha Stele, a black basalt inscription found at Dhiban, Jordan, in 1868 and now in the Louvre. In it King Mesha of Moab, about 840 BC, says Chemosh had been angry with his land and let Israel's king Omri oppress it, then gave Moab victory. It is one of the longest inscriptions in a language close to biblical Hebrew, and it shows how Moab spoke of its own god (compare 2 Kings 3:4–27).

Jewish law later formalized conversion: immersion, acceptance of the commandments and, for men, circumcision. The Talmud (Yevamot 47b) reads Naomi's attempts to send Ruth back as the warnings given to a would-be convert, and each part of Ruth's vow as her acceptance of a part of the law: "where you go" as the Sabbath limits on travel, "where you spend the night" as the rules against a man and woman being alone together, "your people" as the commandments, "your God" as rejecting idols, and "where you die" and "there I will be buried" as the law's penalties and burial rules. Because of Ruth, converts to Judaism are often given the Hebrew name Ruth or called children of Abraham and Sarah.

deep.title: Wandering widows in other ancient stories
deep.b: There is no close parallel to Ruth in surviving Egyptian, Mesopotamian or Canaanite literature. Ancient laws, such as the Middle Assyrian Laws and the Hittite Laws, do deal with widows and brothers-in-law, and a Ugaritic poem from about 1300 BC praises a ruler, Danel, who "judges the case of the widow." These show the customs Ruth assumes, but the story itself, a foreign widow choosing her mother-in-law's people and God, has no known model.

echoes: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 12:10; Genesis 19:30–38; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Judges 21:25; Exodus 15:23–25; Job 1:21; Isaiah 56:3–7

settings.to: Orpah and Ruth, her widowed Moabite daughters-in-law
settings.when: on the road from Moab to Judah, as Naomi sends them back
settings.why: Naomi asks the LORD to show them the faithful love (hesed) they showed to the dead and to her. She asks him to give each of them rest in a new husband's house. It is the first blessing in the book, and the rest of the story answers it: the LORD's faithful love comes through people, and Ruth finds rest in Boaz's house. An Israelite widow blessing Moabite women in the LORD's name would strike readers who knew Deuteronomy 23:3–6.

settings.when: after they insist on going with her
settings.why: Naomi argues that she has no more sons to marry them, and that waiting would be foolish. She says the LORD's hand has gone out against her. The speech assumes the custom of brother-in-law marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) and shows how hopeless she thinks things are. Orpah's return is sensible; Ruth's refusal is beyond what anyone could ask.

settings.to: Naomi, her widowed mother-in-law, on the road from Moab to Judah
settings.when: after Naomi has urged both her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' homes, and Orpah has gone
settings.why: Ruth answers Naomi's three pleas to turn back by binding herself to Naomi's people, her God and even her grave, sealed with an oath in the name of the LORD. For an Israelite reader, a Moabite swearing by the LORD would be striking, because Deuteronomy 23:3 kept Moabites out of the assembly.

settings.when: on her arrival home, when the women ask, "Can this be Naomi?"
settings.why: Naomi, Pleasant, asks to be called Mara, Bitter. "Full I went out, and empty the LORD has brought me back" (1:21). She speaks like Job, blaming the Almighty openly. She does not count Ruth, who stands beside her. The lament sets up the whole story, which will fill her emptiness, and the same women will bless her in 4:14–15.

title: The Field of Boaz
sum: Ruth goes out to glean, gathering leftover grain behind the harvesters, as Israel's law allowed the poor, the foreigner and the widow. "As chance would have it," she ends up in the field of Boaz, a man of worth from Elimelech's clan. Boaz notices her, protects her, feeds her at his own table, and has his men drop extra grain for her. He blesses her: may the LORD, "under whose wings you have come to take refuge," reward her.
Ruth comes home with about an ephah of barley. When Naomi hears the name Boaz, her bitterness breaks: "He is one of our family redeemers." Ruth gleans through the whole barley and wheat harvest.
readings: Read as history

A detailed picture of a village harvest: reapers, a foreman, young women binding sheaves, water jars, a midday meal of bread and sour wine, gleaners at the edges. It shows the gleaning laws (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 24:19–22) working in practice, and the real dangers a foreign woman faced in the fields (2:9, 22).
Read as story

A meeting scene, like the well scenes where Isaac's, Jacob's and Moses' wives are found (Genesis 24; 29; Exodus 2). The storyteller plays with the pattern, and keeps the irony in view: Ruth's "chance" is plainly no accident, and Boaz prays for God's wings to cover her when he is in a position to do it himself.

views.J: Boaz is a righteous judge; some rabbis even identified him with the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem (Judges 12:8–10; Talmud, Bava Batra 91a). The Talmud (Shabbat 113b) says it was the modest way Ruth gleaned that caught his attention. The chapter is a model of hesed: the landowner keeps the law of gleaning and goes far beyond it.
views.T: Boaz, the Lord of the harvest who welcomes a foreign woman, gives her bread and drink, and protects her, has long been read as a picture of Christ. Preachers since the early church have drawn on Boaz's gifts of bread (compare John 6:35) and on the refuge "under his wings" (Matthew 23:37).
views.R: The chapter introduces David's great-grandfather as a capable, generous, God-fearing landowner, with qualities later seen in David's own care for the poor and his loyalty to friends (1 Samuel 30:21–25; 2 Samuel 9:1–7).
views.E: Ruth is called a Moabite three times in this chapter (2:2, 6, 21) and a nokhriyyah, "foreigner" (2:10), the very word used for the foreign wives sent away in Ezra 10. Here an Israelite leader welcomes that "foreigner" and blesses her in the LORD's name.
views.W: Ruth takes the initiative; she does not wait for permission from Naomi or anyone. The chapter also shows the danger of men (2:9, 15, 22) and the importance of women's networks: Boaz's young women protect Ruth, and Naomi's home is where the news is weighed and the next step is planned.

deep.b:
Israel's law set aside part of every harvest. Farmers were not to reap the corners of their fields or go back for sheaves they forgot, and grape and olive pickers were not to strip the vines and trees bare (Leviticus 19:9–10; 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:19–22). These leftovers belonged to the poor, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. The law is tied to Israel's memory: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 24:22).

Gleaning gave the poor a right, not a handout, but it still depended on the owner and his workers. Boaz goes far beyond the law: he lets Ruth glean among the sheaves, feeds her, gives her water, and has extra stalks pulled out for her. The later Mishnah has a whole tractate, Peah ("Corner"), on these rules.

Barley harvest began in about April and wheat harvest ended about seven weeks later, around May or June. The Gezer Calendar, a small limestone tablet from about the 900s BC found at Gezer in 1908, lists the farm year month by month, including "a month of barley harvest" and "a month of harvest and measuring." It is one of the oldest Hebrew inscriptions known.

deep.title: Boaz answers his own prayer
deep.b: This is my own reading, though others have noticed parts of it. Boaz's blessing in 2:12, "under whose wings you have come to take refuge," uses kanaf, wing. Ruth uses the same word in 3:9, "Spread your kanaf over your servant." Her request turns Boaz's prayer into a question for Boaz himself. I think the book is quietly arguing that God's wings over his people often take the shape of a person's cloak: the prayers of the book (1:8–9; 2:12, 19–20; 4:11–12, 14) are all answered through people who choose to act. The pattern is widely noted for 2:12 and 3:9; applying it to every blessing in the book is my extension.

echoes: Leviticus 19:9–10; Leviticus 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:19–22; Genesis 24:11–20; Genesis 29:9–12; Psalm 17:8; Psalm 91:4; Matthew 23:37; Leviticus 25:25

settings.what: Boaz and the harvesters bless each other
settings.by: Boaz, and his harvesters in answer
settings.to: His harvesters in the field; Boaz
settings.why: "The LORD be with you!" "The LORD bless you!" The everyday greeting shows Boaz as a man whose work life is shaped by faith. The rabbis of the Mishnah (tractate Berakhot) took it as a model for greeting others in God's name.

settings.by: The young man in charge of the harvesters
settings.to: Boaz, who asks whose young woman she is
settings.when: as Boaz arrives in his field
settings.why: "She is a young Moabite woman, the one who came back with Naomi" (2:6). It is the first time Bethlehem names her, and it names her by her foreign people. He adds that she asked politely and has worked since morning. The report tells Boaz, and the reader, both what marks her as an outsider and what marks her as worthy.

settings.what: Boaz's protection and his orders to his men
settings.to: Ruth, gleaning in his field; then his young men
settings.when: after he learns who she is, and at mealtime
settings.why: Boaz tells Ruth to stay in his field, near his young women. He has ordered the young men not to touch her, and she may drink from their water. At mealtime he feeds her himself. Then he orders his men to let her glean even among the sheaves, and to pull out stalks for her (2:15–16). The law only left the edges and the dropped grain for the poor (Deuteronomy 24:19). Boaz goes beyond it, and he protects a foreign widow who might be harmed in another field (2:22).

settings.when: when Ruth asks why he notices her, a foreigner
settings.why: Boaz has heard how she left her father, mother and native land for a people she did not know, like Abraham (Genesis 12:1). He asks the LORD to repay her in full. He is the God of Israel, "under whose wings you have come for refuge" (2:12). The blessing names Ruth as one who has taken refuge in Israel's God. Boaz does not yet see that he will be the answer: in 3:9 Ruth asks him to spread the wing of his cloak over her.

settings.what: Naomi's blessing: he is one of our redeemers
settings.to: Ruth, back from the field with an ephah of barley
settings.why: Naomi blesses the man who noticed her. When she hears the name Boaz, she blesses him by the LORD, "who has not abandoned his faithful love for the living and the dead" (2:20). Then she tells Ruth that he is one of their family redeemers. Her bitterness breaks; the woman who said the LORD had turned against her now praises his faithful love. For readers it is the turning point of the story.
views: The Hebrew can mean that the LORD has not abandoned his faithful love, or that Boaz has not. Many readers think the ambiguity is deliberate: God's love is shown through Boaz.

title: Midnight at the Threshing Floor
sum: The harvest is over and nothing has happened. Naomi makes a daring plan: Ruth is to wash, put on perfumed oil, go down to the threshing floor where Boaz sleeps beside his grain, uncover his feet and lie down. At midnight Boaz wakes with a start. Ruth goes beyond the plan: "Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant, because you are a family redeemer."

Boaz blesses her, calls her a "woman of worth," and promises to act, but there is a closer redeemer who has the first right. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley, so that she will not "come to your mother-in-law empty." Naomi tells Ruth to wait: "The man will not rest until he has settled the matter today."
readings: Read as history

A real marriage proposal, made in the only private setting available to a poor widow and a landowner during harvest. The custom of spreading a garment over a woman as a sign of marriage is known from Ezekiel 16:8, and the threshing floor was where owners slept to guard their grain.
Read as story

The most suspenseful scene in the book. The narrator uses words that can be innocent or sexual ("uncover," "feet," "lie down," "know") to make the reader hold their breath, then shows a man and a woman acting with honor. The night scene also answers chapter 2: Boaz's prayer about God's "wings" (2:12) becomes Ruth's request for Boaz's "wing" (3:9). The scene also recalls Lot and his daughters, the origin of Moab (Genesis 19:30–38): an older man who has eaten and drunk, a younger woman's night initiative to save a family line. Harold Fisch traced this pattern from Lot's daughters through Tamar to Ruth; here a Moabite woman re-enacts it with complete honor.
Read as a moral question

Readers have argued about the plan from the beginning. Was it a risky but honorable proposal, a trap set by Naomi, or a scandal the story covers over? The text gives Boaz the last word: "This last act of faithful love is even greater than the first."

views.J: The rabbis held up Boaz as a hero of self-control, comparing him to Joseph (Ruth Rabbah). They also read Ruth's preparations as signs of conversion: washing from idolatry, oil as the commandments, clothes as Sabbath clothes (Rashi). The six measures became six righteous descendants, including David and the Messiah (Targum; Sanhedrin 93a–b).
views.T: A favorite picture of the believer coming to Christ: Ruth comes at night, lies at his feet, and asks for his covering, and the redeemer promises, "I will do for you everything you ask" (3:11; compare John 6:37). The "wing" is often linked to Malachi's "a sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings" (Malachi 4:2).
views.R: Boaz's insistence on law and public process (3:12–13) protects the legitimacy of David's ancestors. Conservative scholars stress that the narrator takes care to show that nothing improper happened, since David's enemies could have used any scandal in his family line.
views.E: The narrator never lets the reader forget that the woman at Boaz's feet is a Moabite, the kind of wife Nehemiah later drove out after Deuteronomy 23:3 was read aloud (Nehemiah 13:1–3, 23–27). On this reading, the most honorable person on the threshing floor is exactly the foreigner such reforms feared.
views.W: This is a woman's plan carried out by a woman who improves on it. Ruth does not wait for Boaz to tell her what to do (3:4); she tells him. Feminist readers note both her courage and her risk: a foreign woman alone at night among men, whose safety depends entirely on one man's character.

deep.b:
After the harvest, sheaves were carried to a threshing floor, beaten or trampled, and then winnowed: tossed into the wind so the light chaff blew away and the heavy grain fell back. Evening winds were best for this. The owner often stayed overnight to guard the grain from thieves.

The place had a mixed reputation. Hosea accuses Israel of loving "the pay of a prostitute on every threshing floor" (Hosea 9:1), perhaps because harvest festivals involved drinking and fertility rites. But threshing floors could also be holy: the angel of the LORD stood at the threshing floor of Araunah, and David bought it for the altar where the temple was later built (2 Samuel 24:16–25; 2 Chronicles 3:1). So the setting carries both danger and promise.

Ancient Israel had several laws that touched widows and inheritance: levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), redemption of land (Leviticus 25:25–34), the inheritance of daughters when there were no sons (Numbers 27:1–11), and the protection of widows and orphans (Exodus 22:22–24). None of these says that a go'el must marry a widow. Ruth's request in 3:9 joins them in a way the law does not, which is why scholars debate whether she is appealing to a local custom or making a new and creative claim.

deep.title: The night at Gibeah and the night at the threshing floor
deep.body: This is my own proposal, building on links others have noticed. Judges ends with two stories about Bethlehem (Judges 17–18; 19–21). In the second, a woman from Bethlehem is handed over to a mob at night in Gibeah, abused until morning, and found dead at the door. Ruth is set "in the days when the judges ruled" and also centers on a woman, Bethlehem, and a night that lasts "until morning" (3:13–14). I think the threshing-floor scene is meant to be read against Gibeah: a vulnerable woman alone with a man at night, and the man protects her, blesses her and sends her home safe at dawn. Gibeah was Saul's town (1 Samuel 10:26); Bethlehem was David's. Scholars have long noted that Judges 17–21 and Ruth both point to the need for a king; reading the two nights as a deliberate pair is my own step, and it rests on shared setting and language more than on any direct quotation.

echoes: Ezekiel 16:8; Deuteronomy 22:30; Genesis 19:30–38; Genesis 38:14–26; Leviticus 25:48–49; Proverbs 31:10; Hosea 9:1; 2 Samuel 24:18–25

settings.when: at the end of the barley and wheat harvests
settings.why: Naomi seeks rest for Ruth, answering her own blessing of 1:9. She sends her to the threshing floor at night, washed and perfumed. Ruth is to uncover Boaz's feet and lie down. The plan is daring and risky. It puts Ruth's good name in Boaz's hands and shows Naomi acting, not only waiting.

Ruth goes beyond Naomi's plan. She names herself and asks Boaz to spread the wing of his cloak over her, because he is a family redeemer. It is a request for marriage, in the words of Boaz's own blessing (2:12) and of Ezekiel 16:8. By naming the redeemer's duty, she joins marriage to the redemption of Elimelech's family.

settings.to: Ruth, at his feet on the threshing floor
settings.why: Boaz blesses her: this act of faithful love is greater than the first, because she did not go after younger men. He calls her a "woman of worth," the same words used of him (2:1). He promises to act, but there is a nearer redeemer. He swears by the LORD that if the other will not redeem her, he will. The oath turns a risky night into a public promise.

settings.when: at dawn, as Ruth comes home with six measures of barley
settings.why: Ruth reports Boaz's words, "Do not come to your mother-in-law empty." They answer Naomi's complaint that the LORD brought her back empty (1:21). Naomi tells her to wait, because the man will not rest until the matter is settled today.

title: A Son Is Born to Naomi
sum: Boaz goes to the town gate, stops the nearer redeemer ("So-and-so"), and gathers ten elders. Naomi's land is for sale, and the man agrees to redeem it, until Boaz adds that whoever buys it takes on Ruth too, to raise up a son in Mahlon's name. The man backs out, hands over his sandal, and Boaz buys the land and marries Ruth before witnesses. The town blesses them: may Ruth be like Rachel and Leah, and Boaz's house like the house of Perez.

The LORD lets Ruth become pregnant, and she bears a son. The women bless God for giving Naomi a redeemer, and they name the boy Obed. He becomes the grandfather of David. A ten-name family line from Perez to David closes the book.
readings: Read as history

A legal scene at the gate, with elders, a property transfer, an old sandal custom explained for later readers, and a marriage announced before witnesses. The closing genealogy, paralleled in 1 Chronicles 2 and Matthew 1, places the family in Israel's royal history.
Read as story

Every loss in chapter 1 is answered. The empty woman holds a child in her lap. The dead man's name is raised up. The town that asked "Can this be Naomi?" now cries "A son is born to Naomi!" The man who would not keep a name alive is left nameless, and the book's last word is David.
Read as theology

The narrator says for only the second time that God acted directly: "the LORD let her become pregnant" (4:13). Human loyalty and law and God's gift work together. The family redeemer turns out to be not only Boaz but the child, who will "bring back" Naomi's life.

views.J: Ruth is the mother of royalty. The Talmud says Ruth lived to see Solomon (Bava Batra 91b), and the line to David is why the book is read at Shavuot, the traditional anniversary of David's birth and death. Obed's birth ends Naomi's exile and shows how a convert can become the ancestor of the Messiah, son of David.
views.T: Boaz pays the price that the nearer redeemer would not, and takes a foreign bride to give life to the dead man's name, a picture for many Christians of Christ the Redeemer and his church. Matthew includes Ruth in Jesus' family tree (Matthew 1:5), and Bethlehem, Ruth's new home, becomes the birthplace of David's greater son (Luke 2:4–11).
views.R: The goal of the book: David's family line. On this view, held by many conservative and some critical scholars, the book was written in or soon after David's time to show that his Moabite ancestry was honorable and that God had guided his family. The sandal custom explained in 4:7 shows a writer looking back some generations.
views.E: A Moabite woman is blessed at the town gate, the very "assembly" from which Deuteronomy 23:3 seemed to bar Moabites, and becomes David's great-grandmother. For scholars who date the book after the exile, this is the book's quiet answer to Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13: Israel's greatest king had a foreign mother in his family.
views.W: Women frame the ending: the women bless, the women declare the son to be Naomi's, the women name him. Yet the genealogy lists only men. Feminist readers note both the remarkable honor given to Ruth and Naomi and how quickly the official record writes them out.

deep.b:
Chapter 4 mixes three customs that the law keeps separate. Redemption of land (Leviticus 25:25): a near relative buys back family land so it stays in the clan. Levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10): a dead man's brother marries his widow, and their first son carries the dead man's name. The sandal (4:7): an old way of confirming a transfer of rights, different from the shaming in Deuteronomy 25:9.

Boaz links the land and the marriage, and the nearer redeemer accepts that link as binding. Scholars disagree on whether this reflects a real custom of the time that went beyond the written law, Boaz's clever use of public pressure, or the storyteller's simplification. All agree that the result keeps the land and the name of Elimelech's family together.

The genealogy in 4:18–22 appears again in 1 Chronicles 2:5–15, with small differences in spelling (Salma for Salmon). Matthew 1:3–6 and Luke 3:31–33 also follow it. Matthew adds that Salmon's wife was Rahab, which is not stated in the Old Testament. On the gaps in the list, see the note at 4:21.

Ruth is one of the five Megillot (scrolls) read in the synagogue at festivals: Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth at Shavuot, Lamentations on the Ninth of Av, Ecclesiastes at Sukkot, and Esther at Purim. Reasons given for reading Ruth at Shavuot include its harvest setting, its link to David (by tradition born and died on Shavuot), and Ruth's acceptance of the Torah, which matches Israel's acceptance of the law at Sinai, celebrated on that festival.

deep.title: Orpah and So-and-so: the reasonable ones
deep.b: This is my own reading, though the contrast between these characters is widely noted. The book has two people who do the sensible, legal, unblamed thing and then vanish: Orpah, who goes home when told to (1:14–15), and the nearer redeemer, who declines a costly duty (4:6). Neither is criticized. Each is matched with a partner who goes further: Ruth stays, Boaz pays. I think the book uses these pairs to define hesed by contrast: it is not doing wrong versus doing right, but doing what is reasonable versus doing more than anyone could ask. The one who goes back has a name and disappears; the one who refuses loses even his name.

echoes: Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Leviticus 25:25; Genesis 38:27–30; Genesis 29:31–30:24; 1 Chronicles 2:5–15; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; Matthew 1:3–6; Luke 3:31–33; Psalm 19:7

settings.to: The nearer redeemer ("So-and-so"), before ten elders of Bethlehem at the town gate
settings.when: the morning after the threshing floor
settings.why: Boaz offers Naomi's field to the nearer redeemer, who agrees to buy it. Then Boaz adds that the buyer also acquires Ruth the Moabite, to raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance. The man backs out, for fear of harming his own inheritance. The scene is a legal hearing before witnesses. It joins the law of redeeming land (Leviticus 25:25) with something like brother-in-law marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). For readers, it shows Boaz doing more than the law requires.
views: Scholars debate how the redemption of land and the marriage were joined, since the Torah does not link them. Some think the custom in Ruth is older or local. Others think the author joined them on purpose.

The written Hebrew (Ketiv) of 4:5 can be read "I acquire Ruth." Then Boaz may be announcing his own marriage, so that the land alone is offered to the other man. Beattie and others argue for this reading (see the variant note on 4:5).

settings.to: The elders and all the people at the gate
settings.when: after the nearer redeemer hands over his sandal
settings.why: "Today you are witnesses" (4:9). Boaz declares that he is acquiring everything of Elimelech and his sons. He is also acquiring Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's wife, to raise up the dead man's name so it will not be cut off. The public act makes the redemption legal and binding. 4:7 explains the sandal custom to later readers who no longer knew it.

settings.what: The blessing of the elders and the people
settings.by: All the people at the gate and the elders
settings.to: Boaz, and through him Ruth, the woman coming into his house
settings.why: They pray that the LORD make Ruth like Rachel and Leah, who built the house of Israel. They pray that Boaz's house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah. The blessing gives the Moabite a place among the mothers of Israel. It also points to Tamar, a widow probably from Canaan, who kept a dead man's line alive (Genesis 38). And it points to Perez, ancestor of Boaz and David (4:18–22). For readers under David's kings, it shows the town blessing the beginning of his family.

settings.to: Naomi, after Ruth bears a son
settings.why: "Blessed be the LORD, who has not let you lack a family redeemer this day!" (4:14). The same women who heard Naomi's bitter lament (1:19–21) now praise God for filling her emptiness. They say the child will bring back her life. And they name what Naomi never said: Ruth, who loves her, is worth more to her than seven sons. The blessing answers the book's opening and honors the Moabite daughter-in-law.

"A son is born to Naomi!" The neighbors name him Obed, and the narrator adds that he was the father of Jesse, the father of David. Only here is a child named by women who are not his mother. The naming ties the story of one family to the house of Israel's king.

traditions.q: Boaz pays to redeem. When Christ redeems, what does he pay, and to whom?
views: The price is Christ's own life, but it was not paid to the devil, nor demanded by the Father to satisfy anger, as Gregory of Nazianzus argued (Oration 45.22). Christ redeems by uniting human nature to God and destroying death from within.

Christ freely offered his life to the Father in love, as a sacrifice that makes satisfaction for our sins (Catechism 613–617). Following Anselm and Thomas Aquinas, Catholics speak of satisfaction rather than of the Father punishing the Son.

In our place Christ kept the law and suffered its curse, and his obedience is counted as ours (Formula of Concord, article 3). Luther called it a happy exchange: Christ takes our sin, and we receive his righteousness.

Christ bore the punishment that God's justice required for his people's sins and fully satisfied it (Westminster Confession 8.5; Heidelberg Catechism 12–18). This penal substitution is at the center of Reformed teaching on the cross.
